Great progress on the `electrum` endpoint today. Updated all tests with version conditions, for initial availability, additions, behavior changes, and obsolescence. Implemented `server.features` and `server.ping` methods. Improved electrum test harness and expanded coverage.

Also verified `bs<-bs` and `bs<-core` full chain and multi-channel sync on `windows` and `linux` and on `manual` and `inbound` channels (most sync we test has been multiple outbound channels over the Internet). Performance looks excellent. Getting close to being able to provide clean benchmarks for blocks out, with the expectation that we should be able to provide the full chain out as fast as we can sync it in.

elements.text: Finished up the tx population query, which populates previous outputs for unconfirmed txs and augments with prevout height and mtp and spender height metadata, allowing the tx to be fully validated, dos checked, and tested for confirmability, using the chain::transaction check/accept/connect/confirm methods. Implemented most of the four electrum payment address methods, as well as the newer "scripthash" address methods that replace them. These are implemented using the same asynchronous technique developed for the native interface, since these queries are arbitrarily large. These are:

1 cancellable
2 cancel when the channel closes
3 use the same parallelizable store methods as native
4 parallelize when

is configured (no parameter option)

The four legacy methods (using p2pkh and p2sh addresses as keys) are identical to the newer scripthash-based methods after address conversion (the sha256 hash of the output script is derivable from p2pkh/p2sh addresses). So the four older methods and newer methods each perform their own version validations and then just pass into common code for the bulk of the implementation.

elements.text:
It will require that the subscription performs the costly computation against block state. This requires sorting all unique parent txs of all confirmed inputs/outputs hitting an address by their height and order within the block, and combining all of those tx hashes into a sha256 midstate. Because this becomes stateful, cumulative, and not reversible, a reorg impacting the address requires it to be rebuilt. The midstate for each subscribed address can then be updated with confirmations.

Since a different sort is used for unconfirmed txs, these cannot be accumulated and must instead be recalculated in full for each notification. Since tx pooling would not result in additional indexation of the same spend upon confirmation, and thus address index is not indexed by confirmation status, this implies independent tracking of pooled txs impacting a subscribed address, so that the this status field can be computed (hash combined with the confirmed midstate)
6. Next, with mempool transactions in the specified order, append a similar string.
The only mempool consistency requirement is that we provide the same transactions upon request as have been hashed into the status.
if the transaction has at least one unconfirmed input, and

if all inputs are confirmed.
5. Order mempool transactions by
height txs, and secondarily the txid (endianness same as human-readable hex string used for display) is used to arrive at a canonical ordering.

So there's that as well. For reasonable numbers of spends for a given address (like 1000), just performing the full computation on each notification isn't so bad. And I suspect that Electrum servers don't actually support large address notifications.

But it's not worth doing if it's going to be broken. The above non-pool implementation is simple enough, and the performance hit for large addresses will only be encountered by the initial subscription (and notification following address reorg) - similar in cost to a full history or balance query.

Adding the pool behavior will require either accumulating unconfirmed tx surrogate keys in each address subscription map, or querying for it dynamically against the unconfirmed tx metadata graph. There's no requirement to pull up old unconfirmed txs that have been stored, just as with the graph. We can pull them up at graph init if we want, but ignoring them causes no harm.

It will require that the subscription performs the costly computation against block state. This requires sorting all unique parent txs of all confirmed inputs/outputs hitting an address by their height and order within the block, and combining all of those tx hashes into a sha256 midstate. Because this becomes stateful, cumulative, and not reversible, a reorg impacting the address requires it to be rebuilt. The midstate for each subscribed address can then be updated with confirmations.

Since a different sort is used for unconfirmed txs, these cannot be accumulated and must instead be recalculated in full for each notification. Since tx pooling would not result in additional indexation of the same spend upon confirmation, and thus address index is not indexed by confirmation status, this implies independent tracking of pooled txs impacting a subscribed address, so that the this status field can be computed (hash combined with the confirmed midstate)

>  6. Next, with mempool transactions in the specified order, append a similar string.
The only mempool consistency requirement is that we provide the same transactions upon request as have been hashed into the status.

>  4. For mempool transactions, we define *height* to be `-1` if the transaction has at least one unconfirmed input, and `0` if all inputs are confirmed.
> 5. Order mempool transactions by `(-height, tx_hash)`, that is, `0` height txs come before `-1` height txs, and secondarily the txid (endianness same as human-readable hex string used for display) is used to arrive at a canonical ordering.
So there's that as well. For reasonable numbers of spends for a given address (like 1000), just performing the full computation on each notification isn't so bad. And I suspect that Electrum servers don't actually support large address notifications.

But it's not worth doing if it's going to be broken. The above non-pool implementation is simple enough, and the performance hit for large addresses will only be encountered by the initial subscription (and notification following address reorg) - similar in cost to a full history or balance query.

Adding the pool behavior will require either accumulating unconfirmed tx surrogate keys in each address subscription map, or querying for it dynamically against the unconfirmed tx metadata graph. There's no requirement to pull up old unconfirmed txs that have been stored, just as with the graph. We can pull them up at graph init if we want, but ignoring them causes no harm.

elements.text:
I managed to complete the 8 electrum non-subscription address methods, including their rpc serialization, complex sorting, and cancellable/asynchronous behavior. Just have to write the four corresponding database queries, which are similar to the existing native queries, and then test the 8 methods, 4 queries, and 3 sorts. That'll take another day.

Then it's on to the address/scripthash (basically the same) subscription/notification. I did get some work done on the address "status" optimization. I set up a copyable midstate struct that allows incremental forward updates to the confirmed aspect of the status hash.  This is a stack allocated 208 bytes that can be held in the channel with each corresponding address subscription. So if you subscribe to an address with 5 million txs, we only compute that once and then just add new spend/receive txs to the hash as they occur.

This might seem uncommon, but I was clicking randomly through the block explorer today and hit an address with 750,000 transactions. Chrome can't handle that amount of json, so we have to process address output enumerations differently, like by using the data or text accept type.

After a quick trip to `PubKey NYC` I've been back on the electrum interface for the last couple days. I had some discussion with `Electrum` folks and decided to drop in the major additions for their WIP on network protocol `v1.7`. Also spent a couple days working of some test and organizational backlog.

That's complete now, as is the database queries and endpoint implementation for the address queries (`balance`, `history`, `mempool`, `listunspent`). These are addressable via `p2pkh`/`p2sh` addresses (only) in early versions, via `output script hash` in current versions, and via `output script` in the next version. We just map all three on to `output script hash`.

The new `outpoint` method is mostly complete, and this adds a subscriber. There are also subscribers for the three address methods above. Most of the work for those is done. That and connection of the fee estimator to its method, and the electrum interface will be complete.

Building Mixed Arm64/x64 Applications
To build an application that utilizes x64 libraries on an Arm build, developers must use Visual Studio 2022 (version 17.3 or later) with the Arm64EC tools enabled.
 The process involves configuring the project to build specific parts as Arm64EC while keeping others as standard x64, ensuring the solution links against the correct versions of dependencies.
Configuration: In the Visual Studio Configuration Manager, create a new platform by selecting Arm64EC and copying settings from x64.
CMake Setup: For CMake projects, add a configuration in
flag to combine the Arm64 and x64 artifacts into a single binary that can run on Arm64 devices.
Dependencies: Ensure external libraries are linked against their x64 or Arm64EC versions; if a library is only available as x64, it will run under emulation within the Arm64EC process.

text:
Building Mixed Arm64/x64 Applications
To build an application that utilizes x64 libraries on an Arm build, developers must use Visual Studio 2022 (version 17.3 or later) with the Arm64EC tools enabled.
 The process involves configuring the project to build specific parts as Arm64EC while keeping others as standard x64, ensuring the solution links against the correct versions of dependencies.

1. Configuration: In the Visual Studio Configuration Manager, create a new platform by selecting Arm64EC and copying settings from x64. 
1. CMake Setup: For CMake projects, add a configuration in `CMakePresets.json` with `"architecture": { "value": "arm64ec", "strategy": "external" }` and set environment variables `CXXFLAGS` and `CFLAGS` to `/arm64EC`. 
1. Linking: When linking, use the `/machine:arm64x` flag to combine the Arm64 and x64 artifacts into a single binary that can run on Arm64 devices. 
2. 
3. Dependencies: Ensure external libraries are linked against their x64 or Arm64EC versions; if a library is only available as x64, it will run under emulation within the Arm64EC process.

text:
Boost links these files based on a single header in its base header library, called `auto_link.hpp`. It constructs the lib path in parts, including this:
```#if defined( _M_IX86 )
#  define BOOST_LIB_ARCH_AND_MODEL_OPT "-x32"
#elif defined( _M_X64 )
#  define BOOST_LIB_ARCH_AND_MODEL_OPT "-x64"
#elif defined( _M_ARM )
#  define BOOST_LIB_ARCH_AND_MODEL_OPT "-a32"
#elif defined( _M_ARM64 )
#  define BOOST_LIB_ARCH_AND_MODEL_OPT "-a64"
#endif

...
#if defined(BOOST_LIB_NAME) \
      && defined(BOOST_LIB_PREFIX) \
      && defined(BOOST_LIB_TOOLSET) \
      && defined(BOOST_LIB_THREAD_OPT) \
      && defined(BOOST_LIB_RT_OPT) \
      && defined(BOOST_LIB_ARCH_AND_MODEL_OPT) \
      && defined(BOOST_LIB_VERSION)```
So when `_M_ARM64` is defined (it is) boost switches to `-a64`. The issue is simply that these libs are not in the NuGet package. But good to know that boost does expect and therefore build them. I could probably copy the x64 into the expected path and link with ARM64EC.

elements.text:
Just completed the implementations of Electrum address/scripthash/scriptpubkey/outpoint subscription/unsubscription/notification. Took me a full day to cleanly satisfy the various  concurrency requirements, but once it was done it finally looked simple again.

The key insight was to (1) use an independent strand for notifications and updates to the notification map, (2) post subscript/unsubscribe from the main channel strand into the notification strand, and (3) post notification sends from the notification strand to the channel strand. This allows the notifications to be simply iterate in a for loop, posting into the notification strand buffer, and allows one request to run concurrently with the notification loop.

This not only protects the map during iteration and updates, and the socket during sends, but also keeps the socket active during the potentially long-running notification queries and loop. The queries are themselves cancellable, and this combination gives us immediate stop initiated by channel close and therefore also for node close.

Previously I had done something similar for long-running non-notification address queries, but that was initiated by the caller, on the socket, not a block or tx organized event originating from the node on an independent strand or even threadpool. So in that case it was necessary to post to an independent thread, establish a socket monitor (to capture socket cancellation), run the long cancellable query, and post the results back the channel strand, releasing the monitor.

But this doesn't satisfy the requirements of an independent job showing up at any time when the socket is either listening or even processing a request, and when the channel strand may be attempting to modify the subscription map. It was getting ugly, and this made it simple again. One strand for incoming callers, and one strand for outgoing notifications, and both bounding to/from the other like magic. :)

Just completed the implementations of Electrum address/scripthash/scriptpubkey/outpoint subscription/unsubscription/notification. Took me a full day to cleanly satisfy the various  concurrency requirements, but once it was done it finally looked simple again.

The key insight was to (1) use an independent strand for notifications and updates to the notification map, (2) post subscript/unsubscribe from the main channel strand into the notification strand, and (3) post notification sends from the notification strand to the channel strand. This allows the notifications to be simply iterate in a for loop, posting into the notification strand buffer, and allows one request to run concurrently with the notification loop.

This not only protects the map during iteration and updates, and the socket during sends, but also keeps the socket active during the potentially long-running notification queries and loop. The queries are themselves cancellable, and this combination gives us immediate stop initiated by channel close and therefore also for node close.

Previously I had done something similar for long-running non-notification address queries, but that was initiated by the caller, on the socket, not a block or tx organized event originating from the node on an independent strand or even threadpool. So in that case it was necessary to post to an independent thread, establish a socket monitor (to capture socket cancellation), run the long cancellable query, and post the results back the channel strand, releasing the monitor.

But this doesn't satisfy the requirements of an independent job showing up at any time when the socket is either listening or even processing a request, and when the channel strand may be attempting to modify the subscription map. It was getting ugly, and this made it simple again. One strand for incoming callers, and one strand for outgoing notifications, and both bounding to/from the other like magic. :)

elements.text: A nice benefit of this approach was that that notification map does not have to be copied and doesn't require any guards to be safely iterated, despite callers attempting to update it. Copy-free, lock-free, and the socket remains active. The one case where the caller will get blocked is when we are processing a notification and the caller is attempting to make a subscription or desubscription. In this case the channel strand posts to the notification strand and while the notifications are being process, the update job just sits in the queue. Once the notifications clear and the update job executes, its completion handler reestablishes the socket listener. But this is exactly what we want to happen. We are busy responding to the caller with notifications from a new event, and the caller is waiting to complete his new subscription/desubscription only during that time. And of course the channels are entirely independent of each other, so everything keeps moving. The server remains fully protected against DoS, as the callers do not control the rate or volume of notifications.

elements.text: Tomorrow is a significant optimization between the server and database in terms of computing electrum address status (ordered hash of all address history). I've implemented midstate hash caching maintained in each subscription at the server protocol object, with an address table surrogate key for the head of the last iteration applied to the midstate. The hash preimage requires an ordering of all txs creating and spending a given address. There are addresses with 5 million spends, possibly as much as 10 million history entries. Without this caching, just subscribing to an address requires the full query to run for every new block and even every new unconfirmed tx. This is because the notification for any new touch on the address requires the FULL SET of touches to be hashed in order. The ordering is such that a new event can cause a change in the middle of the hash preimage. So even midstate caching gets complex. Yes, this is a crazy design.

text: Tomorrow is a significant optimization between the server and database in terms of computing electrum address status (ordered hash of all address history). I've implemented midstate hash caching maintained in each subscription at the server protocol object, with an address table surrogate key for the head of the last iteration applied to the midstate. The hash preimage requires an ordering of all txs creating and spending a given address. There are addresses with 5 million spends, possibly as much as 10 million history entries. Without this caching, just subscribing to an address requires the full query to run for every new block and even every new unconfirmed tx. This is because the notification for any new touch on the address requires the FULL SET of touches to be hashed in order. The ordering is such that a new event can cause a change in the middle of the hash preimage. So even midstate caching gets complex. Yes, this is a crazy design.

elements.text:
So the approach is to rely on the relative stability of confirmed history, and recompute unconfirmed history on each even. Fortunately the sort places confirmed history first in the preimage. The simple approach is to wipe the midstate cache whenever there is a reorganization (confirmed block height reduced), because the midstate cannot be rolled back.

The address hash table is a multimap, which allows iteration from the bucket to the end of the conflict list (though the iterator skips over conflicts and only exposes matches). So it presents as a stack, with the most recent item at the top (in the hashmap bucket). So we store the top at the start of the iteration, grab all of the entries and spenders, sort by confirmed state, and hash the confirmed ones using the streaming hash accumulator. Once the last confirmed is committed to the accumulator, we save off the accumulator to the subscription, and continue with the unconfirmed.

The set of unconfirmed can change completely given just one new tx in the mix, so there is no benefit in caching. But the number of them is generally trivial by comparison. For the 5M output address there may be zero or one touch unconfirmed. Still, we need to find all of them, and they can be any depth in the stack for a given address. So on the first iteration, we read the entire set. On subsequent iterations, we set the iterator to stop at the previous top, and we read for confirmed entries only. We sort and hash these into the midstate, update the cache, and then read the entire stack for unconfirmed entries. Since this will be updating with each block (at least) the confirmed query will be trivial and require almost no hashing.

The unconfirmed iteration ignores all entries for which the associated tx is not associated to a block (not strong). However it still hits every single element in the conflict list (e.g. 5M). But the cost of this query is dramatically reduced because there are a trivial number of unconfirmed, and new entries require a fee computation prevout confirmedness, and position/height. So basically, by caching the midstate, we still have to run a long iteration, find each tx instance, and check each for confirmation, but overall the query cost is cut dramatically, and the hash cost is eliminated almost entirely.

elements.text: The performance fallback option is to just put a limit on the size of an address that can be subscribed. Because each update essentially requires a cumulative scan of the entire update history, that ultimately becomes necessary. So once the subscription scan hits a certain depth it just errors out and fails the subscription with a specific code. This would be a reasonable precaution for public servers. And since these queries operate over a collection of output links that are accumulated up-front, this is very simple and inexpensive to evaluate.

Also the first notification (server-initiated message) is now integrated into the unit tests, with the unit test sending a node event, causing server subscriptions to evaluate and send as applicable, and then receiving the json-rpc notification. Triggering the notify at the server is just: `notify(node::chase::organized, {});` and handling it is just: `const auto message = receive();` where the message is the json-rpc notification from the server.
